'''Peter Lynn''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FAcSS}} is a British [[statistician]] and professor at the [[University of Essex]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Peter Lynn at ISER, University of Essex|url= https://www.iser.essex.ac.uk/people/plynn |accessdate=7 December 2025}}</ref> Lynn was previously director of the Institute for Social and Economic Research (2020-2023) and has held the positions of Vice-President (2009-2011) and President (2017-2019) of the [[International Association of Survey Statisticians]]. He is well known for his work on [[Survey methodology|survey design and implementation methods]], particularly for [[Longitudinal study|longitudinal social surveys]], including pioneering work on targeted methods to address survey nonresponse.

==Early life==
Lynn  was educated at [[Crookhorn College|Crookhorn Comprehensive School]] and [[Havant and South Downs College|Havant Sixth Form College]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Peter Lynn CV|url=https://www.iser.essex.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/files/staff/plynn.pdf|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref> before studying statistics, computing and economics at [[University College, London]]. He graduated in 1987 with an [[British undergraduate degree classification#Upper second-class honours|upper second class]] Bachelor of Science (BSc) degree.<ref>{{cite web|title=Essex People: Peter Lynn|url=https://www.essex.ac.uk/people/LYNNP23606/Peter-Lynn|accessdate=8 December 2025}}</ref> Later, he gained a master's degree in applied statistics from [[Sheffield Hallam University]] and Doctor of Philosophy degree from the [[University of Essex]] with a thesis entitled ''Improving the quality of social survey data: a collection of published papers''.<ref>{{cite web|title=Thesis: Peter Lynn|url=https://essex.primo.exlibrisgroup.com/discovery/fulldisplay?docid=alma991005443959707346&context=L&vid=44UOES_INST:UOES&lang=en&search_scope=MyInst_and_CI&adaptor=Local%20Search%20Engine&tab=Everything&query=any,contains,lynn%20peter&offset=0|accessdate=8 December 2025}}</ref>

==Career==
Upon graduation, Lynn joined the [[National Centre for Social Research]] as a survey researcher. In 1994 he was promoted to research director and was, for several years, director of the Scottish School Leavers Survey series, carried out for the Scottish Government. In 1998, he became director of the Survey Methods Centre, a position held for three years before moving to the [[University of Essex]] as Professor of Survey Methodology.<ref>{{cite web|title=Professor Peter Lynn, ISER|url=https://www.iser.essex.ac.uk/people/plynn|accessdate=8 December 2025}}</ref> In 2020, Lynn became director of the Institute for Social and Economic Research.<ref>{{cite web|title=Announcing our new Director – Professor Peter Lynn
|url=https://www.iser.essex.ac.uk/research/news/2020/06/02/announcing-our-new-director-professor-peter-lynn|accessdate=8 December 2025}}</ref>

Lynn headed up the ESRC-funded UK Survey Resources Network from 2008 to 2011<ref>{{cite web|title=New Survey Resources Network|url=https://cls.ucl.ac.uk/new-survey-resources-network/|accessdate=8 December 2025}}</ref> and since 2023 he has been Director of Survey Futures,<ref>{{cite web|title= Survey Futures |url=https://surveyfutures.net/|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref> a sector-wide collaboration to secure the future of social survey data collection in the UK.

In 2004, with [[Willem Saris]], Lynn co-founded the European Survey Research Association and also founded its journal, [[Survey Research Methods]], of which he became the first Editor-in-Chief.<ref>{{cite web|title= Survey Research Methods Editorial Team|url=https://ojs.ub.uni-konstanz.de/srm/about/editorialTeam|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref> He has been involved since its inception in the [[European Social Survey]], having served (1997-1999) on the [[European Science Foundation]] methodology committee to develop a blueprint for the survey.<ref>{{cite web|title= The European Social Survey: a research instrument for the social sciences in Europe|url=http://archives.esf.org/coordinating-research/research-networking-programmes/social-sciences-soc/current-research-networking-programmes/completed-esf-research-networking-programmes-in-the-social-sciences/blueprint-for-a-european-social-survey-ess/the-european-social-survey-a-research-instrument-for-the-social-sciences-in-europe.html|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref> Lynn was subsequently a member of the sampling expert panel, the methodology committee and, since 2017, a member of the Core Scientific Team as Chair of the sampling and weighting expert panel.<ref>{{cite web|title= ESS Structure and Governance|url=https://www.europeansocialsurvey.org/about/structure-and-governance|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref>

He has served on various committees, including the National Statistics Methodology Advisory Committee, the Department for Business, Innovation and Skills Expert Review Group on Evaluation, the Ministry of Justice Court Reform Advisory Panel, and the [[Economic and Social Research Council]] (ESRC) Expert Advisory Group for Data Infrastructure, Skills and Methods.<ref>{{cite web|title=ESRC EAG|url=https://www.ukri.org/who-we-are/esrc/how-we-are-governed/eag/|accessdate=8 December 2025}}</ref> He is currently an advisor to the [[United Nations Statistics Division]] on household survey methods.<ref>{{cite web|title=Revision of the United Nations Handbooks on Household Surveys|url=https://unstats.un.org/iswghs/HandbookRevision|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref> He served as Editor of the ''[[Journal of the Royal Statistical Society]]'' Series A (Statistics in Society) from 2002 to 2005 and as associate editor of the [[Statistics Canada]] journal ''[[Survey Methodology]]'' from 2010 to 2015.

In 2017, he was elected president of the [[International Statistical Institute|International Association of Survey Statisticians]], having earlier served two-year terms as vice-president and president-elect.<ref>{{cite web|title=Professor Peter Lynn: President-Elect of the International Association of Survey Statisticians
|url=https://www.iser.essex.ac.uk/research/news/2015/06/22/professor-peter-lynn-president-elect-of-the-international-association-of-survey-statisticians|accessdate=8 December 2025}}</ref>

==Work==

===Sample design===
One of Lynn's main areas of research has been in the field of sample design for social surveys. An early paper compared the statistical properties of the electoral registers, the main sampling frame used for general population surveys in the UK, with those of the [[Postcode Address File]] (PAF), a new database produced by the Royal Mail. The conclusion was that the PAF had considerable advantages and this prompted most UK surveys to switch to the PAF.<ref>{{cite web|title= On the Bias and Variance of Samples of Individuals|url= https://academic.oup.com/jrsssd/article-abstract/44/2/173/7123231 |accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref> Another influential paper, co-authored with Gerry Nicolaas, assessed the use of random digit dialling – a popular sampling method in the USA - and concluded that it was unsuitable for use in the UK.<ref>{{cite web|title= Random-Digit Dialling in the UK: Viability Revisited|url= https://academic.oup.com/jrsssa/article/165/2/297/7084156|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref> Other contributions on sampling have addressed practical methods to select a sample design based on empirical prediction,<ref>{{cite web|title= Approximations to b* in the prediction of design effects due to clustering|url= https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/en/pub/12-001-x/2005001/article/8093-eng.pdf |accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Design effects for multiple design samples|url= https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/en/pub/12-001-x/2006001/article/9256-eng.pdf|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref> sample designs to achieve equivalence in cross-national surveys,<ref>{{cite web|title=Methods for achieving equivalence of samples in cross-national surveys: the European Social Survey experience|url= https://researchportal.helsinki.fi/en/publications/methods-for-achieving-equivalence-of-samples-in-cross-national-su-2/|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Survey-Based Cross-Country Comparisons Where Countries Vary in Sample Design: Issues and Solutions
|url= https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1515/jos-2017-0007|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref> definitions of representativeness,<ref>{{cite web|title=Commentary: the need for representative survey samples|url= https://www.llcsjournal.org/index.php/llcs/article/view/345/439|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref> and allocation to sampling strata for adaptive survey designs.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Implications of Alternative Allocation Criteria in Adaptive Design for Panel Surveys|url= https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1515/jos-2017-0036|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref>

===Survey nonresponse===
Lynn has made major contributions to the understanding of the nature of survey nonresponse, and to the development of methods to reduce it.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Impact of Incentives on Response Rates to Personal Interview Surveys: Role and Perceptions of Interviewers|url= https://academic.oup.com/ijpor/article-abstract/13/3/326/698402|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Separating refusal bias and non-contact bias: evidence from UK national surveys|url=https://rss.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/1467-9884.00321|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=The Long-Term Effectiveness of Refusal Conversion Procedures on Longitudinal Surveys|url=https://academic.oup.com/jrsssa/article/169/3/459/7085142|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Longer Interviews May Not Affect Subsequent Survey Participation Propensity|url=https://academic.oup.com/poq/article-abstract/78/2/500/2270243|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Targeted Appeals for Participation in Letters to Panel Survey Members|url=https://academic.oup.com/poq/article-abstract/80/3/771/1753474|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref>

===Data collection modes===
A third theme to Lynn’s research corpus is optimal choice of modes of data collection. In the 1990s he contributed to assessment of the emerging method of computer-assisted personal interviewing (CAPI).<ref>{{cite web|title=Data collection mode effects on responses to attitudinal questions|url= https://search.gesis.org/gesis_bib/gesis-bib-28218|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref> He subsequently investigated ways of combining personal and telephone interviewing,<ref>{{cite web|title=The potential of a multi-mode data collection design to reduce non response bias|url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11135-007-9148-5|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Alternative Sequential Mixed-Mode Designs: Effects on Attrition Rates, Attrition Bias, and Costs|url=https://academic.oup.com/jssam/article-abstract/1/2/183/942393|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref> and later contributed to the development of ways to effectively combine web data collection with personal interviews.<ref>{{cite web|title=Going Online with a Face-to-Face Household Panel: Effects of a Mixed Mode Design on Item and Unit Non-Response|url=https://ojs.ub.uni-konstanz.de/srm/article/view/5475|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title= Web-Face-to-Face Mixed-Mode Design in a Longitudinal Survey: Effects on Participation Rates, Sample Composition, and Costs|url= https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1515/jos-2017-0019|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title= Evaluating push-to-web methodology for mixed-mode surveys using address-based samples|url= https://ojs.ub.uni-konstanz.de/srm/article/view/7591|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref>

==Honours==
In 2003, Lynn was awarded the Royal Statistical Society [[Guy Medal]] for services to social surveys.<ref>{{cite web|title=RSS: List of previous winners|url=https://rss.org.uk/RSS/media/File-library/Events/Honours/List-of-previous-winners-2025.pdf/|accessdate=8 December 2025}}</ref> In 2017, he was elected a Fellow of the Academy of Social Sciences.<ref>{{cite web|title=Academy of Social Sciences Names 69 New Fellows|url=https://www.socialsciencespace.com/2017/10/academy-social-sciences-names-69-new-fellows/|accessdate=9 December 2025}}</ref>
